content: St. Louis encephalitis is a moderate infection of the central nervous system caused by the St. Louis encephalitis virus, a Group IV positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Flaviviridae family and the Flavivirus genus. This virus is closely related to other flaviviruses such as Yellow fever virus, Dengue virus, West Nile virus, and Japanese encephalitis virus. It is classified as an arbovirus, meaning it is transmitted by arthropods, primarily mosquitoes, to humans. The virus is typically transmitted to humans through the bite of infected mosquitoes, most commonly from the Culex genus. The incubation period for the disease is approximately 5 to 15 days. Humans are considered dead-end hosts for the virus, as the viral load in the bloodstream is insufficient to infect mosquitoes, and there is no evidence of person-to-person transmission. St. Louis encephalitis must be differentiated from other diseases that present with nonspecific symptoms such as fever, headache, myalgia, and vomiting. These differential diagnoses include meningitis, brain abscess, and demyelinating diseases. The prognosis for St. Louis encephalitis is generally poor, with a mortality rate ranging from 5% to 30%, particularly higher among elderly individuals. Among survivors, approximately 50% experience severe neurological, cognitive, or psychological deficits. The diagnostic method of choice is laboratory testing. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis often reveals moderate lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein levels, which are indicative of neuroinvasive disease. Serologic testing is the primary diagnostic tool in the absence of sensitive and non-invasive viral detection methods. Imaging studies, particularly MRI, may show findings such as edema in the substantia nigra, hemorrhage, and restricted diffusion in the basal ganglia and thalamus. Electroencephalography (EEG) may demonstrate generalized slowing without focal activity, persistent vegetative states, or brain death. There is no specific treatment for St. Louis encephalitis. Management is primarily supportive, focusing on symptom relief and prevention of complications. Surgical intervention is not recommended. Preventative measures include the use of insect repellents, protective clothing, window screens, and efforts to control mosquito populations. There are no vaccines available for St. Louis encephalitis, and no secondary preventative measures exist. The disease was first identified in 1933 by Dr. Joseph F. Bredeck following a major outbreak in St. Louis, Missouri. The causative virus was isolated by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in monkeys and white mice. The incidence of St. Louis encephalitis is approximately 192 cases per 100,000 individuals worldwide, with most cases reported in the United States. The disease affects men and women equally, with no racial predilection, and can occur in individuals of all age groups. However, advanced age, immunosuppression, mosquito exposure, and travel to endemic regions such as Central and South America are significant risk factors. If left untreated, approximately 40% of patients may develop complications such as seizures, coma, disorientation, spastic paralysis, and hemorrhage. The case fatality rate ranges from 5% to 15%, and survivors often face long-term neurological and psychological impairments. Routine screening for St. Louis encephalitis is not recommended due to insufficient evidence, as per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
